text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Sydel v. HMTQ,

2010 BCSC 638

Date: 20100505

Docket:
S097390

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Eva Notburga Marita Sydel

Plaintiff

And

Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, Her Majesty the Queen in Right of British
Columbia, Attorney General for Canada, Attorney General for British Columbia,
Richard Olney, Tim Gohagan, James Morrison, Andrea Berman, Chris Flemming, K.
Bothwick, Pete Dehal, J. Lee, Juergen Leske, C. Lim, Joe M. Majchrowki, Jason
Rauh, Thomas Redden, Joseph Remedios, Daniela Salmen, Robert Schell, Phil
Seagle, Shania Walters, Michael Yiu, D. Kerr, M. Ma, Margaret Ashby, Warren
Cooke, Dale King, David Morgan, Jim Talbot, Bruce Harper, Paul Pellitier, Jana
Hyman, Paul Meyers, Harbans Dhillon, Rosemary Gallagher, Valmond Romilly, Jodie
Werier, John Doe and Jane Doe

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Kelleher

Reasons for Judgment

The Plaintiff, In Person:

E. Sydel

Counsel for the Defendants,
Her Majesty the Queen in Right of
British Columbia, Attorney General for British Columbia, Paul Meyers, Harbans
Dhillon, Rosemary Gallagher,

Valmond Romilly
and Jodie Werier:

T.H. MacLachlan, Q.C.

E. Graff

Counsel for all other named Defendants:

J.W. Levine

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

April 16, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

May
5, 2010

Introduction

[
1
]

Before the Court are two applications brought
pursuant to Rule 19(24) of the
Rules of Court
.  The applicants seek an order
striking the entirety of the plaintiff’s writ and statement of claim without
leave to amend, and an order dismissing her action in its entirety.

[
2
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

(24)      At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b)        it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)        it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
3
]

One of these applications is brought by Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of British Columbia, the Attorney General for
British Columbia, Paul Meyers, Harbans Dhillon, Rosemary Gallagher, Valmond
Romilly and Jodie Werier (the “Provincial Defendants”). Similar relief is
sought in a separate notice of motion filed on behalf of all other named
defendants, who are referred to by the parties as the Federal Defendants.

[
4
]

The plaintiff’s action stems from criminal
proceedings in the Provincial Court of British Columbia.  She was convicted by
the court of four counts of making false statements in her tax returns and five
counts of evading the payment of income tax, contrary to the
Income Tax Act
,
R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.). Briefly put, the plaintiff claims that the
investigation leading up to her convictions and the proceedings before the
Provincial Court were part of a conspiracy against her engaged in by employees
of the Canada Revenue Agency, lawyers employed by the Federal Department of
Justice, and Judges of the Provincial Court.

[
5
]

Ms. Sydel claims that the investigation and
prosecution taken against her were conducted in bad faith and without
jurisdiction, and were improperly motivated by her association with the “detax
movement”, which the Federal Defendants have sought to infiltrate and destroy.
The plaintiff’s position is that the proceedings demonstrate a concerted
strategy of persecution on the part of all the defendants, exemplified in part
by the selection of a Jewish Judge and Prosecutor (given the fact that she is
of German descent), and the fact that individual members of the Federal and
Provincial Defendants are Freemasons who communicated in Masonic sign language
during the course of her trial.

[
6
]

The individual Provincial Defendants are all judges,
members of the Provincial Court of British Columbia.

[
7
]

Ms. Sydel characterizes the allegations made in
her statement of claim as matters of grave national importance.  She says that
they raise the issue of a “secret criminal gang operating inside the
administration of justice in British Columbia”.

[
8
]

Ms. Sydel says the improprieties and abuses set
out in her claim led up to and culminated in her convictions and eventual
incarceration. In this action Ms. Sydel claims $300,000,000.00 in damages, and
seeks declarations that the
Income Tax Act
is invalid and that her
convictions are unlawful and a nullity at law.

[
9
]

The Provincial and Federal Defendants claim that
the plaintiff’s action offends all four subsections of Rule 19(24), and ought
to be struck out on any of the grounds enumerated therein, either individually
or cumulatively. Their overarching complaint is that the plaintiff’s action
constitutes an abuse of this Court’s process and represents an improper
collateral attack on her criminal convictions.

[
10
]

Ms. Sydel opposes the applications.
Additionally she seeks an adjournment of this matter until the hearing of her
appeal from conviction or until such time as various members of the Provincial
and Federal Defendants provide answers to Interrogatories regarding their
association with Freemasonry.

[
11
]

For the reasons that follow, I decline to grant
the adjournment sought by the plaintiff. Further, I find that Ms. Sydel’s
action suffers from fundamental defects which cannot be remedied by an
amendment to her pleadings. Accordingly, the applications of both the
Provincial Defendants and the Federal Defendants are granted, and the
plaintiff’s action is dismissed in its entirety.

Background
Facts

[
12
]

Ms. Sydel’s detailed 135 paragraph statement of
claim sets out a range of allegations against the defendants, all of which
relate directly or indirectly to her convictions for contraventions of the
Income
Tax Act
.

[
13
]

On July 6, 2006, the plaintiff was found guilty
of the offences charged. Ms. Sydel was represented by counsel in those
proceedings. Her substantive defence to the charges was premised in part on a
claim that the
Income Tax Act

is invalid legislation, and on the ground
that she is a “natural person”, and as such is not obliged to pay any income
tax. The defendant, the Honourable Judge Paul Meyers, rejected these
submissions in reasons indexed at
2006 BCPC 346
.

[
14
]

In the course of those reasons, Judge Meyers
expressly found that Ms. Sydel was subject to the provisions of the
Income
Tax Act
, which is valid legislation.

[
15
]

Prior to the formal entry of the convictions,
the plaintiff brought an application seeking a mistrial or a judicial stay of
proceedings before Judge Meyers.

[
16
]

On February 15, 2007, Judge Meyers dismissed
this application and affirmed the convictions. His reasons for doing so are
indexed at
2007 BCPC 50
. In the course of his reasons, Judge Myers expressly
found that the decision to prosecute Ms. Sydel did not exemplify bad faith or
improper motives on the part of the Federal Defendants, and that the plaintiff
was not used as a “poster girl to show the public what happens when you evade
paying taxes.”

[
17
]

On October 19, 2007, the plaintiff was sentenced
to 18 months imprisonment and fined $244,446.78.

[
18
]

Ms. Sydel filed a notice of appeal from her
convictions in this Court. She was granted bail pending the hearing of her
appeal, but never perfected bail and served out two-thirds of her sentence
before being released.

[
19
]

Ms. Sydel subsequently abandoned her appeal, and
on April 17, 2008, Garson J. (as she then was) granted an order dismissing the
appeal as abandoned.

[
20
]

A year and one-half later, Ms. Sydel commenced
the present action, filing a writ of summons on October 8, 2009.

[
21
]

Ms. Sydel’s claims and allegations against the
various defendants can be summarized as follows:

a)

Searches of her residence and her arrest prior
to conviction were improper, without jurisdiction, and in violation of the
Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
;

b)

Judges of the Provincial Court are subject to
intimidation and harassment by Department of Justice lawyers;

c)

The fact that the charges were brought against
her and prosecuted as summary conviction matters violated her rights. This
manner of proceeding removed her right to a jury trial and subjected her to the
“inferior” judiciary of the Provincial Court;

d)

The various Judges of the Provincial Court who
were involved in adjudicating the prosecution brought against her knowingly and
unlawfully acted without jurisdiction;

e)

Her prosecution was selective and actuated by
malice or bad faith, and in breach of the principles of natural justice;

f)

The selection of a Jewish Judge and prosecutor
violated her rights;

g)

The Canada Revenue Agency’s investigation into
the “detax movement” and the plaintiff as an associate of that movement
violated her rights;

h)

Her prosecution violated the
Statutory
Instruments Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-22;

i)

Richard Olney, an employee of the Canada Revenue
Agency, and Judge Meyers are members of the Freemasons, who communicated in
Freemason sign language during the course of judicial proceedings in a
conspiracy against her;

j)

The
Income Tax Act
is invalid
legislation, and her prosecution pursuant to its provisions was a nullity and
taken without jurisdiction; and

k)

The publication of her prosecution and
conviction has defamed her.

[
22
]

After filing the present action, on March 30,
2010, Ms. Sydel filed an application to reinstate and extend the time for
bringing her appeal from conviction. This application has been set down for
hearing on October 1, 2010. That application repeats many of the same
allegations set forth in her statement of claim, including the fact that her
conviction was tainted by improper conduct relating to Freemasonry; that her
conviction was contrary to the
Statutory Instruments Act
; and, that the
Income
Tax Act
is invalid.

Application
for an Adjournment

[
23
]

Before turning to the submissions of the Federal
and Provincial Defendants, I will address Ms. Sydel’s request for an
adjournment.

[
24
]

In
Rose v. University of British Columbia
,

2008 BCSC 1661
, Wilson J. rejected a plaintiff’s adjournment application where
the adjournment sought would serve no meaningful purpose and was incapable of
changing the ultimate result of the hearing:

[18]      In
the course of his submissions in reply, Mr. Rose did seek an adjournment in
order to obtain legal counsel.  Normally that is something the court would
grant to a unrepresented party.  However, in this case I am satisfied that
legal representation will not assist Mr. Rose in the claims put forward in the
Statement of Claim.  I consider it to be incapable of amendment.  Further, Mr.
Rose has had notice of at least one of the applications since August, but did
not advise any of the counsel of his intent to apply for an adjournment to
obtain counsel.  He also gave no information with respect to any particular
counsel having been retained.  I thus conclude that the effect of such an
adjournment would just be to delay the inevitable and to increase the costs to
all of the parties.

[
25
]

Given my ultimate finding that Ms. Sydel’s
claims are fundamentally flawed and incapable of amendment, I reach a similar
conclusion, and deny the plaintiff’s application. An adjournment would simply
delay the inevitable and increase the costs incurred by the defendants and Ms.
Sydel.

Analysis

[
26
]

As noted above, all of the defendants in this
case invoke the entirety of Rule 19(24) in support of their applications
to strike the plaintiff’s claim.

[
27
]

I will begin my analysis with a review of the
plaintiff’s submissions.

[
28
]

As the plaintiff notes, the courts are rightly
reluctant to deprive a plaintiff of the right to pursue her claim. Ms. Sydel
also correctly submits that it is a fundamental principle that “justice must
not only be done, it must be seen to be done”.

[
29
]

Accordingly, unless it is plain and obvious that
the plaintiff’s writ and statement of claim disclose no reasonable cause of
action, an application pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a) cannot succeed. Additionally,
on an application brought pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a), the facts pleaded in a statement
of claim must be taken as true, and no evidence is admissible:
Hunt v. Carey
Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; Rule 19(27).

[
30
]

However, evidence may be adduced with respect to
applications under sub-rules (b) and (d):
Rose
,

at para.
10
.

[
31
]

Ms. Sydel submitted evidence at the hearing of
the applications, in the form of affidavits sworn by her, and by Mr. Kirby
McAllister.

[
32
]

Ms. Sydel’s affidavits are intended to provide
the Court with sufficient facts to demonstrate that her asserted claims possess
an air of reality. To that end, the plaintiff has produced transcripts of other
judicial proceedings and submissions where the validity of the
Income Tax
Act
was attacked.

[
33
]

Mr. McAllister deposes that he is a magician,
and in the course of his career has become familiar with certain hand motions
and gestures. His evidence is that members of the Freemason fraternity
communicate with one another through sign language, though he does not profess
to know how to communicate in this language.

[
34
]

Mr. McAllister was present during the
plaintiff’s bail hearing in Provincial Court, and swears that during the course
of those proceedings he observed the defendants Judge Meyers and Mr. Richard
Olney engage in communication through the use of hand gestures and head
movements.

[
35
]

Ms. Sydel also relies on a notice to admit,
which she says establishes the Provincial Defendants are deemed to have
admitted that some form of secret communication was engaged in at the hearing.
I accept the affidavit material filed by the Province which demonstrates the
notice to admit was properly responded to within the time required by the
Rules.

[
36
]

In addition to her reliance on these materials
to provide an air of reality to her claim, Ms. Sydel submits that when presumed
to be true, her pleadings disclose a valid cause of action and cannot be struck
pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a). The plaintiff disputes the Provincial Defendants’
submission that the doctrine of judicial immunity provides a complete answer to
her claims against them. She claims that
s. 42
of the
Provincial Court Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 379 is
ultra vires
the powers of the provincial
legislature, and says that in any event, the decision in
MacKeigan v.
Hickman
,
1989 CanLII 40 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 796, established that judicial immunity is a
qualified privilege which does not provide protection in cases of judicial
corruption.

[
37
]

The Provincial and Federal Defendants disagree
with Ms. Sydel. In their submission, the allegations raised in the pleadings
could suggest a number of causes of action, including: conspiracy, defamation,
malicious prosecution, and abuse or misfeasance in public office. However, they
note that none of those causes of action can be supported by the facts pled.
The facts alleged do not satisfy the required legal elements of any of these
causes of action.

[
38
]

The defendants submit this is particularly so
when the Court goes behind the pleadings and declines to accept the plaintiff’s
allegations (which they say are based on speculation and assumption) as true.
This is a permissible approach:
Young v. Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
, 64
B.C.L.R. (4th) 157.

[
39
]

While there is considerable merit to this
submission, in my view, it is not necessary to look behind the pleadings and
strike Ms. Sydel’s claim on the grounds that it is plain and obvious it
discloses no cause of action. That is because as there is ample room under the
other subrules of Rule 19(24) to address the difficulties in this case.

[
40
]

Rule 19(24)(d) authorizes the Court to dismiss a
proceeding where the claims advanced are an abuse of the Court’s process. The
discretion afforded courts to dismiss actions on the ground of abuse of process
extends to any circumstance in which the court process is used for an improper
purpose. Proceedings which attempt to utilize the Court’s civil process for an
ulterior or improper purpose may be struck under Rule 19(24)(d):
Babavic v.
Babowech
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.)
.

[
41
]

Pleadings that are a collateral attack on a
pre-existing judgment may constitute an abuse of process under Rule 19(24)(d):
V.H.
v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2005 BCSC 139
at para.
59
.

[
42
]

It is an abuse of the Court’s process to bring a
civil action which attempts to collaterally challenge a criminal conviction. As
a result of the distinction between criminal proceedings and civil litigation,
a party cannot seek a remedy statutorily provided for by way of an appeal
through civil proceedings. Such an evasion of the criminal process is known as
a collateral attack and is prohibited:
Hainsworth v. Ontario (Attorney
General)
,
[2002] O.J. No. 1390 at paras. 39-40 (S.C.J.)
;
Semeniuk v.
British Columbia (Financial Institutions Commission)
,
2008 BCSC 1634
at
para.
26
.

[
43
]

Public policy requires a defendant, who seeks to
challenge her conviction, to do so directly by seeking to appeal that
conviction. As Lord Steyn noted in
Arthur J.S. Hall and Co. v. Simons
,

[2002] 1 A.C. 615 at 679 (H.L.)
:

It is... prima
facie an abuse to initiate a collateral civil challenge to a criminal
conviction. Ordinarily therefore a collateral civil challenge to a criminal
conviction will be struck out as an abuse of process.

[
44
]

The doctrine of collateral attack was described
by Mr. Justice McIntyre of the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Wilson
,

1983 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594 at 599, as follows:

It has long
been a fundamental rule that a court order made by a court having jurisdiction
to make it, stands and is binding and conclusive unless it is set aside on
appeal or lawfully quashed. It is also well settled in the authorities that
such an order may not be attacked collaterally - and a collateral attack may be
described as an attack made in proceedings other than those whose specific
object is the reversal, variation, or nullification of the order or judgment.
Where appeals have been exhausted and other means of direct attack upon a
judgment or order, such as proceedings by prerogative writs or proceedings for
judicial review, have been unavailing, the only recourse open to one who seeks
to set aside a court order is an action for review in the High Court where
grounds for such a proceeding exist.

[
45
]

In
Benji v. Keefer
,
2008 BCSC 1721
, the
plaintiff brought an action against Crown counsel, for alleged misconduct,
abuses, and unbecoming conduct in the course of a murder trial in which the
plaintiff was the accused. The plaintiff had brought a motion to have the
prosecutor removed during the criminal trial. The trial judge dismissed this
application, and her conclusion was not appealed.

[
46
]

On a Rule 19(24) application brought by the
defendant, Chamberlist J. agreed that as the civil action raised “essentially
the same issues” as those argued at the recusal application, the plaintiff had
improperly sought to convert his complaints into a civil cause of action to
support a claim for damages. He concluded it was a collateral attack upon the
earlier ruling of the trial judge and therefore an abuse of process. The Court
also noted that the plaintiff’s real complaint appeared to be that in the
course of the criminal prosecution and trial his rights had been violated to
such an extent that his prosecution amounted to an abuse of process. This
however, did not give rise to a triable issue, as there is no cause of action
for abuse of process which can found a civil lawsuit.

[
47
]

Accordingly, the plaintiff’s claim was struck.

[
48
]

A similar result prevailed in
V.H.
, where
the plaintiff was criminally charged and ultimately pled guilty. The plaintiff
subsequently commenced a civil lawsuit against a variety of justice system
participants and governmental bodies. The court noted at para. 100, “that it
would be an abuse of the process of this Court to now allow the plaintiffs to
litigate in the civil courts the issues in the criminal proceedings...”.

[
49
]

The conclusions in
Benji
and
V.H.

apply
in this case. It is plain that the plaintiff’s claims are actuated by an
ulterior or improper purpose, that purpose being an attempt to challenge the
entirety of the criminal process taken against her in a civil action for
damages.

[
50
]

In so finding, I recognize that the gravamen of
Ms. Sydel’s claim is that the Provincial Court was not a court of competent jurisdiction
and acted in excess of its authority, as the
Income Tax Act
is invalid
legislation. Accordingly, she suggests she is not mounting a collateral attack,
as the proceedings and orders made in the Provincial Court are a nullity and
were
void ab initio
.

[
51
]

I disagree. For the purposes of Rule 19(24)(d),
this Court is not required to assume that arguments of law dressed up as
assertions of material fact are true, or assume that presumptively valid
legislation is in fact non-existent. The plaintiffs’ submissions and pleadings
do not reference a single instance in which a Canadian Court has found that the

Income Tax Act
is void or does not exist at law.

[
52
]

In
Canada (Attorney General) v. Hanover
,

2007 BCSC 1378
at paras.
19-28
, Romilly J. extensively reviewed the many
authorities which have rejected the assertions Ms. Sydel makes and establish
that the
Income Tax Act
is valid legislation.  Accordingly, a Court
proceeding taken pursuant to its provisions is within jurisdiction.

[
53
]

In any event, it is plain and obvious that the
entirety of the plaintiff’s action is based upon issues that were either
litigated in the Provincial Court, or arise out of the conduct of those
proceedings and the investigation which led to their initiation.

[
54
]

In seeking a declaration that her conviction and
sentencing were unlawful and a nullity, challenging the investigation which led
up to the conviction, and challenging the conduct of the proceedings in the
Provincial Court, Ms. Sydel is essentially seeking a rehearing of the issues
determined at her criminal trial. These issues were fully addressed and
rejected in Judge Meyer’s reasons for conviction and his reasons denying the
plaintiff’s application for a judicial stay of proceedings.

[
55
]

Even if I were to accept that the Provincial
Court proceedings were taken without jurisdiction, a civil action for damages
is not an appropriate forum to litigate this issue.

[
56
]

Where an accused seeks such relief, the proper
and only recognized course of action is to appeal the convictions to a court of
competent jurisdiction, not to commence a civil action for damages. In
proceeding to file her writ and statement of claim, Ms. Sydel has mounted a
collateral attack on her criminal convictions, which constitutes an abuse of
the Court’s process. On this basis, I strike the entirety of her action against
all the defendants.

[
57
]

The plaintiff herself appears to recognize that
an appeal is the appropriate forum within which to advance her allegations and
claims.

[
58
]

In her submissions in support of her application
to adjourn this hearing pending her appeal from conviction, the plaintiff
stated that “the outcome of the [criminal] appeal process will determine
whether there is merit to the legal argument of the Federal Government
Defendants and the Provincial Defendants in respect of the Plaintiff’s failure
to appeal her conviction.”

[
59
]

In the application to reinstate her appeal filed
on March 30 of this year, Ms. Sydel raises many of the same allegations set
forth in her statement of claim as grounds of appeal, including the fact that
her conviction was tainted by improper conduct relating to Freemasonry; that
her conviction was contrary to the
Statutory Instruments Act
; and, that
the
Income Tax Act
is invalid.

[
60
]

In summary, I find it is plain and obvious that
the plaintiff’s claims are a collateral attack on prior criminal proceedings
and ought to be struck as an abuse of process pursuant to Rule 19(24)(d). The
appropriate (and only) forum within which Ms. Sydel is entitled to advance an
attack on her convictions and related matters is on appeal.

[
61
]

Accordingly, as no amendment could revive the
plaintiff’s pleadings, which are deficient in a fundamental rather than an
incidental sense, it is appropriate to strike the plaintiff’s claim in its
entirety and dismiss the action.

Costs

[
62
]

The Federal Defendants seek their costs of this
application. The Provincial Defendants have applied for special costs.

[
63
]

While Rule 19(24) expressly contemplates an
award of special costs, I have determined that such an order is not appropriate
at this time although it may be in future if the plaintiff continues to pursue
vexatious litigation in the face of these reasons for judgment.

[
64
]

That said, there is no reason in this case to
depart from the ordinary rule that a successful party is entitled to their
costs. Each group of defendants are entitled to one set of costs at Scale B.

“Mr.
Justice Kelleher”
